body.en: Almost all *enzymes* are proteins; some nucleic acids that behave like enzymes are called ribozymes. An enzyme, like any protein, has a tertiary structure with crevices or pockets; one such pocket where the substrate fits is the active site. Unlike inorganic catalysts, enzymes are damaged at high temperatures (above 40 °C), though enzymes from thermophilic organisms living at 80–90 °C stay stable. Carbonic anhydrase speeds up the reaction CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ about 10 million times.

points.en: Ribozymes: nucleic acids with enzyme activity.
Active site: the pocket into which the substrate fits.
*Enzymes* are not used up in the reaction.

title.en: How an enzyme speeds a reaction

narration.en: Let us draw the energy hill, the enzyme–substrate complex and a real number.

say.en: Without an enzyme, the substrate must climb a high energy hill, the activation energy, before it turns into product.
The enzyme lowers that hill. The start and the end stay the same, so only the rate changes.
The substrate fits the active site, forming a short-lived enzyme–substrate complex. Product is released and the enzyme is free again.
Carbonic anhydrase is a striking case: about 200 carbonic acid molecules form per hour without it, and 600 000 per second with it.
Let us draw the energy hill, the enzyme-substrate complex and a real number.

caption.en: A reaction must climb an energy hill (the activation energy) through a transition state. An enzyme binds the substrate at its active site and offers an easier path with a lower hill. It does not change the start or end energy, only the height of the hill.
caption.kn: ಕ್ರಿಯೆ ಸಂಕ್ರಮಣ ಸ್ಥಿತಿಯ ಮೂಲಕ ಶಕ್ತಿಯ ಬೆಟ್ಟವನ್ನು ಏರಬೇಕು. ಕಿಣ್ವ ಕಡಿಮೆ ಎತ್ತರದ ಸುಲಭ ದಾರಿ ನೀಡುತ್ತದೆ; ಆರಂಭ ಮತ್ತು ಅಂತ್ಯದ ಶಕ್ತಿ ಬದಲಾಗುವುದಿಲ್ಲ.

body.en: A substrate must reach a higher-energy transition state before it becomes product. The energy needed to reach it is the activation energy. *Enzymes* lower the activation energy, so the reaction goes faster; they do not change the energy difference between substrate and product. The enzyme binds the substrate (S) at its active site to form a short-lived enzyme–substrate complex (ES), which changes into an enzyme–product complex (EP) and releases the product, freeing the enzyme for another substrate molecule.

points.en: E + S ⇌ ES → EP → E + P

problem.en: Without the enzyme about 200 molecules of H₂CO₃ form in an hour; with carbonic anhydrase about 600,000 form every second. Estimate how many times faster the catalysed reaction is.

steps.en: Uncatalysed rate: 200 per hour = 200 ÷ 3600 ≈ 0.056 molecules per second.

narration.en: Let us work through this together. Without the enzyme about 200 molecules of H₂CO₃ form in an hour; with carbonic anhydrase about 600,000 form every second. Estimate how many times faster the catalysed reaction is.

say.en: Let us work through this together. Without the enzyme about 200 molecules of H 2CO 3 form in an hour; with carbonic anhydrase about 600,000 form every second. Estimate how many times faster the catalysed reaction is.
Uncatalysed rate: 200 per hour equals 200 divided by 3600 is approximately 0.056 molecules per second.
Catalysed rate: 600,000 per second.
Ratio equals 600,000 divided by 0.056 is approximately 1.08 times 10 to the power 7, about 10 million times.
So the answer is About 10 million times faster.
